title: Brian Walker - Procedural level design in Brogue and beyond
speaker: Brian Walker
summary: Brian Walker, creator of Brogue, walks step by step through Brogue's level generator: room accretion with varied room shapes, adding loops to break the perfect tree, cellular-automata lakes placed only where they don't disconnect the level, terrain features, and especially 'machines' - loosely specified set pieces like key altars, reward rooms, vestibules and goblin warrens that the generator fits into choke-point regions of an existing layout. He then describes an unnamed roguelike platformer inspired by Super Metroid, with movement-scaled time, jump pathfinding, fixes for inescapable pits, gravity-driven gases and liquids, structural collapse, and a single giant cellular-automata map with one-way shortcut doors. In Q&A he discusses choke-point analysis, tolerating edge-case failures except ones that block progress, and why Brogue added seeds.

insights.claim: Procedural levels are central to roguelikes because they shift the skill curve to mastering systems and adapting rather than memorising levels, and because each level feels like a real place discovered for the first time.
insights.detail: Walker says with a 32-bit seed probably no one has seen your level before. As a developer, seeing new levels lets him approach his own game with novelty, where static-game developers may need more outside playtesters.
insights.quote: the skill curve is more about mastering the systems of the game learning how to adapt to what you're given

insights.claim: Procedural level design is a different, not easier, skill from hand-placing levels: you build systems, generate, judge which output feels better, and tweak parameters over years.
insights.detail: Rather than laying out elements like an artist on a canvas, you iterate by trying an idea and tweaking hyperparameters. Walker says it is not a time-saver. In Q&A he adds that most of Brogue's development time went into tweaking level generation, which he calls the most exciting part of roguelike development.
insights.quote: you come up with an idea you try it you tweak the the hyper parameters for four years

insights.claim: Brogue builds its level skeleton by room accretion: generate a room (overlapping rectangles, cellular-automata blob, or circle, optionally with a hallway) and attach it where it fits snugly against an existing room through a door without overlap.
insights.detail: Cellular automata start from a random grid (e.g. 50% wall) and flip cells surrounded by a majority of the opposite type, with thresholds controlling density and smoothness. Each room picks door candidates on each side; the generator scans level locations in random order until the new room fits, repeating until the level is full.
insights.quote: you start with a room you add another room on to it and you keep doing that until the level is full

insights.claim: Brogue fixes room accretion's perfect-tree layout by adding doors through any wall tile whose two opposite floor sides are far apart by path distance.
insights.detail: A pure tree has exactly one non-backtracking path between any two points, which is easy to get cornered in and causes backtracking. Walker scans walls in random order and converts one to a door when the pathing distance between the floors on either side is large enough, yielding a densely connected level.
insights.quote: find wall tiles that have a floor on each of the two opposite sides and if the pathing distance between those two floor tiles is large enough

insights.claim: Brogue adds level-wide features like lakes and chasms as cellular-automata blobs, brute-force checking each placement and only placing it if it would not disconnect any walkable tiles.
insights.detail: Walker wanted global-scale features so players can see across the level, affect and be affected by distant things, and spot secret doors they can't yet reach. Lakes may overlap and get liquid types assigned afterwards. Then many interactive terrain features are placed: luminescent fungus, grass, torches, dangerous foliage, things that burn, explode or emit gas.
insights.quote: it blocks the level if you put it somewhere and that makes any pair of walkable tiles inaccessible to one another

insights.claim: Brogue's key-altar machines create spatial puzzles, such as a room of dry grass where taking the key drops a torch that ignites the grass near the exit.
insights.detail: The fire spreads toward the player, who must teleport, blink, use fire immunity or find already-burned ground. Other examples: monsters bursting from statues when the key is lifted, and a lava field crossed via fire immunity, levitation or a hidden lever, with the lava evaporating once the key is taken. Each plays out differently depending on monsters and health.
insights.quote: the player runs over to the altar and grabs the key and the torch falls off the wall and ignites the grass near the entrance

insights.claim: Brogue interlocks machines across a level so that keys, locked rooms and set pieces in different areas form a globally coherent structure of concrete goals.
insights.detail: In an example level, a key on a walkway hidden by chasm traps and a key stolen by a monkey open two reward rooms, while a vampire lair's key opens a vault with a magic weapon. Walker says this isn't narrative in the sense Tarn Adams discussed earlier but a physical structure where the whole level interlocks.
insights.quote: the level is kind of globally coherent like they're elements from all parts of the level that tie into the other parts

insights.claim: Brogue's reward rooms let players take exactly one of several items, and are generated on a rubber band so their pace is roughly constant across games, helping players assemble a competent character.
insights.detail: Items are only accessible while all are in place, so you can swap your choice by putting one back. Generation probability rises each time a reward room is not generated and drops when one is.
insights.quote: the probability goes up every time one is not generated and drops down when one is so you get roughly the same pace of reward rooms

insights.claim: Brogue specifies machines as minimal qualitative relationships (room full of grass, altar distant, torch near, line of sight, minimum counts) rather than fixed grids, so they fit into existing layouts and stay unpredictable.
insights.detail: The generator takes the accreted skeleton, picks a spot, and turns it into a machine. Because they aren't predefined stamps, players can't see the first tile and know the whole room, and different machines can look similar at the outset.
insights.quote: you define it with the minimum amount of specification that you need to make the machine work

insights.claim: To build an organic winding path between two points, fill the area with obstructing terrain one cell at a time in random order, skipping any cell that would block connectivity, until only a single meandering path remains.
insights.detail: Brogue uses this for bridges, tunnels through granite and pathways between traps.
insights.quote: you just build obstructive terrain everywhere in random order one cell at a time and you don't build it if it would block the level

insights.claim: Brogue places room and vestibule machines by analysing the level for choke points that dominate a set number of cells, then may reshape or even fully regenerate that region.
insights.detail: Room machines use a single point dominating enough cells, sometimes widened with cellular automata; vestibule machines capture the area just outside a room's door (glyph-triggered statues, guarded walkways, flammable barricades); area machines need no enclosure. In the walkthrough, a choke point dominating a large area becomes a goblin warren by rerunning room accretion with narrower, claustrophobic rooms. In Q&A Walker explains computing choke points by retracting the level cell by cell from the farthest point while counting cells absorbed.
insights.quote: it just kind of analyzes the level and finds a place where there's a single a single point that dominates a certain number of other points

insights.claim: Brogue aligns up-stairs with the previous level's down-stairs for spatial continuity, and places stairs in dead-end alcoves so stepping onto them can mean using them, removing the need for a separate command.
insights.detail: It picks spots walled on all sides but one, where that open side is not a choke point or hallway, so there is no other reason to enter the tile.
insights.quote: it tries to pick a spot for stairs where you don't like there's no reason to step on that space except to use the stairs

insights.claim: Walker's roguelike platformer keeps play cerebral by freezing time when the player stands still, scaling time with ground movement, and allowing slow motion.
insights.detail: Taking a page from Braid without rewinding: time is frozen when motionless on the ground and not using items, passes normally in the air or when using an item, and passes proportionally to ground speed. Players can toggle slow motion for complicated manoeuvres. Inspired by Super Metroid, it is one giant level from top to bottom.
insights.quote: if you're motionless standing on the ground not using any items than time is frozen automatically

insights.claim: Pathfinding in a procedural platformer is much harder than on a grid, so Walker leans on flying enemies and teleporters since ground monsters get stuck and auto-travel is impractical.
insights.detail: The key is an algorithm deciding whether one point can be jumped to from another, which is finicky given headroom and obstacles, and making creatures actually execute it is harder still. He never got it perfect.
insights.quote: you often need a lot of flying enemies because there it's easier to get ground-based enemies kind of stuck in the platforming

insights.claim: To prevent inescapable pits in a procedural platformer, run pathfinding from the level entrance and add platforms wherever a reachable cell sits above a cell from which the start cannot be reached, repeating until all is passable.
insights.detail: Walker calls these 'wells of doom'. Iterating guarantees, to the accuracy of the jump pathfinding, that the player cannot get stuck.
insights.quote: you have to prevent these kind of wells of doom or you can fall down into a pit and you can't jump back out

insights.claim: Gravity breaks the up/down symmetry of top-down roguelikes, enabling dynamic terrain like spreading vines, buoyant or heavy gases, falling liquids, liquid interactions and structural collapse.
insights.detail: Liquids can fall and evaporate, terrain can emit or absorb gases and liquids, doors hold them back until opened, and lava plus water makes steam. A Brogue-style machine floods lava with water vents to fill a room with steam, where survival depends on room shape. Structural support is easy to compute and see, so explosions can sever platforms that then collapse, akin to Dwarf Fortress cave-ins.
insights.quote: in a platformer gravity means that up and down is like feels qualitatively different and plays different from left and right

insights.claim: Walker's platformer generates one huge cellular-automata cave, connects disconnected regions, uses distance from the start as a proxy for depth, and adds hidden one-way shortcut doors that open from the far side, like Super Metroid.
insights.detail: Connecting doors are vertical or horizontal and designed for gravity. Monster spawning by depth becomes spawning by distance from start. Shortcut doors are completely hidden until discovered from the far side, so exploration channels players down one path that later loops back. The full map takes about as long as a typical roguelike.
insights.quote: instead of sort of depth level like wraiths can spawn on depths 8 through 15 or whatever and in a roguelike you just use distance from the start

insights.claim: A generator can tolerate occasional edge-case failures like an inaccessible reward room, but must never produce one that blocks progress, such as an unreachable down-staircase.
insights.detail: Walker's philosophy: if it works in 100% of cases you aren't being ambitious enough. Always check that downstairs are reachable from upstairs, and never let level passability depend on destructible terrain. In the platformer, explosives come late alongside mobility items, teleporters and extra lives as safety valves; players who deliberately break the level accept the result.
insights.quote: you can afford an occasional edge case failure what you can't afford is an edge case failure that like completely blocks the player from progress

insights.claim: Brogue's seed feature, now used for online seed contests where everyone plays the same levels, was originally built so players could send seeds to debug rare level-generation edge cases.
insights.detail: For bugs appearing maybe one in ten thousand times, Walker would ask for the seed and step through generation to find what went wrong.
insights.quote: I originally came up with that because I needed to debug all of these like obnoxious edge cases
